prompt: A PR refactors the `RewardsService` API. The author says: "I'll update the README and method comments in a follow-up CL." Best response?
choices: Fine — docs reviews should be separate so code review stays focused
Only the header comments must change now; READMEs can follow later
Fine, as long as a follow-up issue is filed and linked from the PR
Ask for the README and method docs to be updated in this same CL
explain: Docs changes belong in the same changelist as the code — separate doc CLs get forgotten and lose context, and reviewers benefit from seeing both together.

prompt: While editing a component you find a README section describing a sync flow you're fairly sure no longer exists, but nobody can confirm. What's the recommended move?
choices: Delete it — when in doubt, default toward removal
Leave it alone since you're not 100% certain
Rewrite it from your best guess of how it works now
Leave it but add a "may be outdated" warning banner
explain: Dead documentation misleads and erodes trust. Remove content you know is wrong, and when in doubt default toward removal.

prompt:
Which header comment best documents this method?

```cpp
std::optional<PublisherInfo> GetPublisherInfo(const std::string& id);
```
choices: `// Returns nullopt if |id| isn't in the local DB. No network fetch; UI thread only.`
`// See https://github.com/brave/brave-core/pull/1234 for the design and details.`
`// Looks up |id| in publisher_map_, then calls ConvertRow() on the result.`
`// Gets the publisher info.`
explain: Method docs should describe the contract — behavior, params, return values, gotchas and restrictions (e.g. threading, staleness) — not restate the name or narrate the implementation.

prompt: You're creating a new major directory, `brave/browser/brave_rewards/`. What should its README.md contain?
choices: A full class-by-class design doc covering every edge case
Purpose, key files, main API usage, and maintainers
Just a title for now; it'll be filled in once the code stabilizes
Nothing — header comments are enough documentation
explain: A README orients newcomers: purpose, key files, main API usage, and maintainers — starting with the simplest use case and building up.

prompt: A Brave doc on adding feature flags copies Chromium's step-by-step instructions verbatim. How should it be written?
choices: Keep the copy so readers don't have to leave the Brave docs
Copy the instructions but add a "last synced" date
Link to the Chromium guide plus a short Brave-specific note
Delete the doc entirely; Brave devs should know upstream docs exist
explain: Duplicated docs drift out of sync. Link to the canonical source and add only the project-specific context (e.g. also register in `brave/browser/about_flags.cc`).

prompt: You're adding a new entry to `docs/best-practices/coding-standards.md`. A reviewer suggests ending it with "See PR #4567 and the Chromium style guide for details." Best response?
choices: Accept — linking beats duplicating, as for all docs
Decline: best-practice entries must be self-contained
Accept, but link only to the PR, not external docs
Copy the entire Chromium style guide section into the entry instead
explain: Best-practice entries are the exception to "link, don't duplicate": distill the relevant rule, rationale, caveats and examples directly, with no links to PRs, other entries or external docs.

prompt: Your team proposes a 40-page comprehensive design doc for a feature, but nobody is assigned to keep it updated. Best advice?
choices: Skip docs entirely and rely on code comments
Write the full doc now; even partly stale, comprehensive beats minimal
Write a small, accurate doc you'll actually maintain
Write the full doc and mark it "historical" when it goes stale
explain: A little fresh documentation beats lots of stale documentation. Treat docs like a bonsai: alive but frequently trimmed, focused on what saves the most developer time.
